_about: Vassals and tributaries that Cliopatria does not record, each with its sources (owner, 2026-11-10: "Yes, do that next", to "Do vassals and tribute next, including the Mongol yoke over Russia?"; then "Yes, add them", to "Add the Ottoman and Qing vassals in these stripes next?").

scripts/derive-cliopatria.mjs adds these to cliopatria.topojson's ties, beside Cliopatria's own vassalage and allegiance rows; the political map draws a tie as stripes in the overlord's color over the vassal (src/render/states.js, src/render/base.js).

vassal and overlord are written exactly as Cliopatria names the states. An overlord list is read in order: the first of them on the map in a year takes the tie (Cliopatria draws the Golden Horde inside the Mongol Empire to 1293, and from 1294 as its own state). A vassal list gives each of Cliopatria's names for one vassal, a tie for each (it calls Kartli the Kingdom of Georgia in some years and the Kingdom of Kartli in others). Cliopatria's own names can mislead: its Serbian Empire after 1371 is Moravian Serbia and then the Serbian Despotate, and its Đại Việt to 1682 is the Mạc dynasty; each row's why says so.

from and to bound the tie, both years included; it is drawn only in the years both states are on the map. kind: tribute | vassal | allegiance | protectorate (each in its sources' word). A tie broken and renewed is one row per stretch.

Cliopatria draws no Rus' principality from 1241 to 1293 except Novgorod and Pskov (from 1285): their lands are inside the Mongol Empire in those years, so the yoke shows from 1285 for Novgorod and from 1294 for the rest.

ties.why: Ruled by the khan's patent and paid his tribute; from Ivan I (1325-1340) its princes collected the tribute of the other Russian principalities for the khans. Muscovy stopped paying in the 1470s (1476), and the khans' overlordship ended officially with the stand on the Ugra in 1480.
One of the principalities the invasion of 1237-1241 made vassals; its grand-princely title was the khan's to give. Tribute to 1480, as for Moscow.

Its prince Mikhail was executed at the Horde in 1318, its rising of 1327 crushed, and after 1382 its princes submitted to Khan Tokhtamysh. The overlordship over the Russian lands ended in 1480; Moscow annexed Tver in 1485.
Its princes took the throne by the khan's patent and submitted to Tokhtamysh after 1382; Moscow annexed the principality in 1392 (Cliopatria draws it to 1394).
A northeastern Rus' principality, tributary as the others were (the general sources); subjugated by Muscovy in 1389. Cliopatria draws it to 1343.

Never taken by the Mongols, but in the winter of 1258/59 Alexander Nevsky and the Horde's troops put down the city's opposition to the tribute, which it then paid. Moscow annexed the republic in 1478 (Cliopatria draws it to 1481).

Daniel of Galicia went to Sarai in the winter of 1245/46 to submit to Batu as a vassal, and his house paid the Horde tribute; still tributary in 1308-1323. The Polish conquest of 1349 ended the vassalage.
After the Battle of Maritsa (1371) John V swore allegiance to Murad I as his vassal. In 1394 Manuel II refused the tribute and Bayezid laid siege to Constantinople, until Timur defeated him in 1402.
In February 1424 Manuel II made Byzantium a vassal of the Ottomans again, for 300,000 silver coins a year, until the fall of Constantinople in 1453.

Mircea the Elder submitted to Sultan Mehmed I in 1417 and agreed to an annual tribute. The suzerainty lasted to the mid-19th century, with interruptions: Vlad III (1456-1462) defied the sultan by refusing the tribute.
Under the sultan again after Vlad III, until Michael the Brave (1593-1601), who rose against the Ottomans.
Under the sultan again after Michael the Brave, to the union with Moldavia in 1859 (its article's infobox: an Ottoman vassal 1417-1862, with interruptions).

In 1498 Stephen the Great agreed to keep paying tribute to Bayezid II. Its article's infobox dates the vassalage 1498-1572, 1574-1600 and 1618-1859 (a Polish vassal 1601-1618); the map follows those spans.
The infobox's second span (after the revolt of John the Terrible, 1572-1574).
The infobox's third span, after Moldavia's years as a Polish vassal (1601-1618), to the union with Wallachia in 1859.

John Zapolya swore fealty to Suleiman on 19 August 1529, and the sultan later recognized his son John II as king and his vassal. The Treaty of Speyer (1570) ended the kingdom; its eastern part went on as the Principality of Transylvania.

An autonomous principality under Ottoman suzerainty, paying the Porte an annual tribute, governed by native princes until 1690, when the Habsburgs' Diploma Leopoldinum put it under Vienna (the Ottomans gave it up at Karlowitz in 1699).

A treaty of 1458 made the city a tributary of the sultan (12,500 gold coins a year from 1481). After 1684, under Habsburg protection as well, it went on recognizing Ottoman sovereignty until the French abolished the Republic in 1808 (Cliopatria draws it to 1806).

In 1475 Ottoman forces under Gedik Ahmed Pasha took the Genoese ports of the Crimea, and thenceforth the khanate was a protectorate of the Ottoman Empire. It paid no tribute; from 1524 the sultan appointed its khans. The Treaty of Kucuk Kaynarca (1774) ended the protectorate.

Cliopatria's own record of Joseon's allegiance to the Ming ends in 1571, but Joseon kept its tributary relations with the Ming until the Qing invasion of 1636-37. Its kind stays Cliopatria's word, allegiance, so the legend does not change in 1572.

On its surrender in January 1637 Joseon had to sever its relationship with the Ming, give up the Ming seals and send the Qing tribute every year; its tributary relations lasted until 1895. Cliopatria names the Qing state the Later Jin Dynasty to 1644, and draws Joseon to 1859.

At Dolon Nor (Duolun) in May 1691 the Kangxi Emperor called the Khalkha chiefs together, and they acknowledged Manchu overlordship in return for protection against the Dzungars; Outer Mongolia declared its independence in December 1911. Cliopatria draws the Khalkha to 1695.

The Qing ruled Tibet from 1720 to 1912. Its article's infobox calls it a protectorate and territory of the Qing dynasty, and its text notes that the Qing word for it, fanbu, is usually translated as vassal. Cliopatria draws Tibet to 1793.

Cliopatria keeps the name Serbian Empire after 1371 for Prince Lazar's Moravian Serbia and then the Serbian Despotate. After Kosovo (1389), Lazar's widow Milica accepted Ottoman suzerainty in the summer of 1390; her son Stefan fought as an Ottoman vassal until the Battle of Ankara (1402), after which his state became the Serbian Despotate.
After a dispute in 1408, Despot Stefan accepted Ottoman vassalage again in 1409; the Ottomans took Smederevo, the capital, on 18 August 1439.
The Peace of Szeged (1444) restored the Despotate, officially an Ottoman vassal in 1447-48 and paying tribute in 1457, until the Ottomans took it on 20 June 1459 (Cliopatria draws it to 1458).

After the Battle of Chernomen (26 September 1371) the Bulgarian tsar was forced to become an Ottoman vassal. Ivan Shishman later reneged, provoking the invasions of 1388 and 1393, when Tarnovo fell after a three-month siege.
In 1428 Lê Lợi established a tributary relationship with the Ming, which lasted until Mạc Đăng Dung took the throne on 15 June 1527.

After 1540 the Ming received tribute from both the restored Lê, then in the south, and the Mạc; the Ming recognized the Lê monarch in 1597. Cliopatria draws the Lê to 1571, and the realm the Lê emperors kept under the Trịnh lords after that (see trinh-ming).

Cliopatria's Đại Việt is the Mạc dynasty (Hanoi to 1592, then its last holdout at Cao Bằng). In 1540 the Ming downgraded Mạc Đăng Dung from emperor to governor (đô thống sứ) and took tribute from the Mạc as from the Lê.

After the Southern Ming both the Lê and the Mạc became tributaries of the Qing (the Mạc article's infobox gives 1662-1677); in 1667 the Kangxi Emperor demanded that Cao Bằng be returned to the Mạc, whose dynasty ended in 1677.

From 1572 Cliopatria draws the realm of the restored Lê emperors as the Trịnh lords, who ran their court; that court sent the tribute (the Trịnh treated the Qing 'as they had treated the Ming Emperors, sending tribute', its article says; only the Lê ruler met China's envoys).

In 1667 the Kangxi Emperor named the Lê emperor King of Annam (An Nam Quốc Vương); the Lê court under the Trịnh paid tribute to the Qing as it had to the Ming, until the Trịnh fell in 1787 (the Lê dynasty ended in 1789).

In 1789 the Qianlong Emperor re-established the tributary relationship and made Nguyễn Huệ King of Annam; its article's infobox gives the Qing tributary years as 1789-1802, when the Nguyễn took Thăng Long.

Kartli (which Cliopatria calls the Kingdom of Georgia in 1468-1578, 1706-1737 and 1744-1802) and Kakheti. The Peace of Amasya (29 May 1555) left eastern Georgia to Iran, under native vassal princes; both kingdoms' articles date their Persian vassalage 1555-1578.
The Ottoman invasion of 1578 made Kartli and Kakheti Ottoman vassals (Kakheti paid a yearly tribute of 30 bales of silk) until 1612; Cliopatria draws no Georgian kingdom from 1579 to 1611.
Persian vassals again from 1612 (both kingdoms' infoboxes: 1612-1723); from 1632 the shah appointed Kartli's kings, and the Treaty of Zuhab (1639) reconfirmed Kartli and Kakheti as Iranian domains.
Ottoman vassals 1723-1736 (both infoboxes; the Treaty of Constantinople of 1724 gave Georgia back to the Ottomans) until Nader Shah drove them out; in 1736 the Ottomans gave up Kartli and Kakheti.

Vassals of Nader Shah's Iran 1736-1747 (both infoboxes); in 1744 he gave Kartli to Teimuraz II and Kakheti to Erekle II, and on his death in 1747 they declared their de facto independence. Cliopatria draws eastern Georgia inside Afsharid Iran from 1738 to 1743.
Kartli and Kakheti united under Erekle II in 1762; he tendered his de jure submission to Karim Khan Zand and received his investiture as vali (its article's infobox: 1762-1763).
The Treaty of Georgievsk (24 July 1783) made Kartli-Kakheti a Russian protectorate, renouncing any dependence on Iran; Paul I annexed it by decree on 18 December 1800 (confirmed 12 September 1801).

left_out.why: Its article does not say it paid the Horde; from 1399 it recognized Moscow's suzerainty.
Cliopatria draws Ryazan only from 1453 (its land is inside the Golden Horde before), and its article has Ivan of Ryazan (1427-1456) renouncing his allegiance to the Horde, with no year.
Its article mentions a campaign of 1340 over unpaid tribute but gives no span; Lithuania took the city between 1395 and 1404.
Moldavia paid the sultan tribute at times from the 1450s (Petru Aron); its article's infobox starts the vassalage in 1498, and the map follows the infobox.
Nominally under the Lê emperor in the north; their articles give them no tribute or investiture of their own.
Cliopatria's Đại Việt from 1683 to 1793 is a small piece of the far south, not the Mạc; no tie is drawn on it.

left_out.state: Despotate of Vidin and Despotate of Dobruja
left_out.why: Their articles give no years for an Ottoman vassalage: Vidin fell to the Ottomans after Nicopolis (1396), and Dobruja was incorporated in 1411.
Only a category on its article calls it an Ottoman vassal; the text gives no years.

left_out.state: Kingdom of Imereti, Principality of Mingrelia, Principality of Guria
left_out.why: The Peace of Amasya (1555) put western Georgia in the Ottoman sphere under native vassal princes, and Guria owed the Porte a yearly tribute from 1614, but no source found says when these ties ended.

mongol-invasion.title: Mongol invasion of Kievan Rus' (Wikipedia; "Tatar yoke" leads there)
mongol-invasion.supports: After the invasion of 1237-1241 the Rus' principalities became vassals and paid tribute; Galicia-Volhynia, Polotsk and Novgorod well into the 14th century; the demands of tribute from Russian princes continued until about 1480.

loc-muscovy.title: Russia: A Country Study, "Muscovy" (Library of Congress, Federal Research Division, 1996)
loc-muscovy.supports: Ivan I (1325-1340) collected tribute from the other Russian principalities for the khans; Mongol overlordship ended officially in 1480; Novgorod conquered in 1478, Tver in 1485.

ugra.title: Great Stand on the Ugra River (Wikipedia)
ugra.supports: 8 October - 11 November 1480; read in Russia as the end of the Tatar yoke, which some historians dispute; Russia officially stopped paying tribute in 1476 (Halperin: sometime in the 1470s).

gh-timeline.title: Timeline of the Golden Horde (Wikipedia)
gh-timeline.supports: Winter 1258/59: in the Novgorod Republic, Alexander Nevsky and the Golden Horde's troops suppress opposition to tribute.

novgorod.title: Novgorod Republic (Wikipedia)
novgorod.supports: Alexander Nevsky agreed to pay tribute; the republic ended in 1478.

tver.title: Principality of Tver (Wikipedia)
tver.supports: Mikhail of Tver executed at the Horde (1318); the anti-Tatar uprising of 1327 crushed; after 1382 the princes of Tver and Nizhny Novgorod submitted to Tokhtamysh; annexed by Moscow in 1485.

nizhny.title: Principality of Nizhny Novgorod-Suzdal (Wikipedia)
nizhny.supports: Its princes received the patent for the throne from the khan; annexed by Moscow in 1392.

byzantium.title: Byzantine Empire under the Palaiologos dynasty (Wikipedia)
byzantium.supports: After Maritsa (1371) John V swore allegiance as a vassal to Murad; Manuel II refused the tribute and Bayezid's siege began in 1394; in February 1424 Manuel II re-established Byzantium as a vassal of the Ottomans (300,000 silver coins a year); to the fall of Constantinople, 1453.

loc-romania.title: Romania: A Country Study, "The Ottoman Invasions" (Library of Congress, Federal Research Division)
loc-romania.supports: In 1417 Mircea capitulated to Sultan Mehmed I and agreed to an annual tribute; Vlad Tepes (1456-62) defied the sultan by refusing to pay tribute; Michael the Brave (1593-1601); after 1541 Transylvania an autonomous principality under Ottoman suzerainty, paying the Porte an annual tribute as a vassal; native princes governed it from 1540 to 1690.

wallachia.title: Wallachia (Wikipedia)
wallachia.supports: In 1417 Wallachia was forced to accept Ottoman suzerainty, which lasted until the mid-19th century, with interruptions brought about by local rulers (Michael the Brave among them); in 1859 Wallachia united with Moldavia (the infobox: Ottoman vassal 1417-1862, with interruptions).

moldavia.title: Moldavia (Wikipedia)
moldavia.supports: Infobox: Ottoman vassal 1498-1572, 1574-1600, 1618-1859; Polish vassal 1601-1618. Body: in 1498 Stephen the Great agreed to continue paying tribute to Bayezid II; Moldavia united with Wallachia in 1859.

eastern-hungary.title: Eastern Hungarian Kingdom (Wikipedia)
eastern-hungary.supports: John I swore fealty to the sultan on 19 August 1529; Suleiman recognized John II as king and his vassal; the Treaty of Speyer (16 August 1570) ended the kingdom.

transylvania.title: Principality of Transylvania (1570-1711) (Wikipedia)
transylvania.supports: An Ottoman vassal state for the majority of the 16th and 17th centuries; the Diploma Leopoldinum (1690); formally attached to Habsburg Hungary after the Treaty of Karlowitz (1699).

ragusa.title: Republic of Ragusa (Wikipedia)
ragusa.supports: The treaty of 1458 made it a tributary of the sultan (12,500 gold coins a year from 1481); in 1684 it continued to recognize the sovereignty of the Ottomans; Marshal Marmont abolished the Republic in 1808 (the infobox gives the Ottoman Empire 1458-1684, with a Habsburg protectorate from 1684).

crimea.title: Crimean Khanate (Wikipedia)
crimea.supports: In 1475 Ottoman forces under Gedik Ahmet Pasha conquered the Crimean coast, and thenceforth the khanate was a protectorate of the Ottoman Empire; it paid no tribute; the sultan appointed its khans from 1524; the Treaty of Kucuk Kaynarca, 1774.

joseon.title: Joseon (Wikipedia)
joseon.supports: Infobox: tributary relations with the Ming and Qing, 1401-1895.

joseon-qing.title: Qing invasion of Joseon (Wikipedia)
joseon-qing.supports: 9 December 1636 - 30 January 1637; Joseon switched its tributary allegiance from the Ming to the Qing, formally severing its relationship with the Ming, gave up the Ming seals of investiture and had to send tributes every year.

mongolia-qing.title: Mongolia under Qing rule (Wikipedia)
mongolia-qing.supports: The Khalkha submitted to the Qing dynasty in 1691, at a congress at Duolun where the Khalkha khans formally declared allegiance; Outer Mongolia declared its independence in December 1911 (infobox).

loc-mongolia.title: Mongolia: A Country Study (Library of Congress, Federal Research Division)
loc-mongolia.supports: In May 1691 the Kangxi Emperor called a kuriltai of Khalkha chiefs at Dolonnur; those present acknowledged Manchu overlordship in return for protection against the Dzungar.

tibet-qing.title: Tibet under Qing rule (Wikipedia)
tibet-qing.supports: The Qing ruled Tibet from 1720 to 1912; the infobox calls it a protectorate and territory of the Qing dynasty; the Qing term fanbu has usually been translated as vassal; Western historians have called it a protectorate, vassal state or tributary.

moravian-serbia.title: Moravian Serbia (Wikipedia)
moravian-serbia.supports: In the summer of 1390 Milica accepted Ottoman suzerainty; Stefan fought as an Ottoman vassal to the Battle of Ankara (1402), after which his state became the Serbian Despotate; infobox: vassal state of the Ottoman Empire, 1390-1402.

serbian-despotate.title: Serbian Despotate (Wikipedia)
serbian-despotate.supports: Serbia a vassal Ottoman state after Kosovo (1390 or 1391); in 1409 Stefan accepted Ottoman vassalage after the dispute of 1408; Smederevo fell on 18 August 1439; restored by the Peace of Szeged (1444); officially an Ottoman vassal in 1447-48; tribute in 1457; conquered on 20 June 1459.

bulgaria.title: Second Bulgarian Empire (Wikipedia)
bulgaria.supports: After the Battle of Chernomen (26 September 1371) the Bulgarian monarch was forced to become an Ottoman vassal; Ivan Shishman later reneged, provoking the invasions of 1388 and 1393; Tarnovo taken after a three-month siege.

le-dynasty.title: Lê dynasty (Wikipedia)
le-dynasty.supports: In 1428 Lê Lợi established a tributary relationship with the Ming; Mạc Đăng Dung took the throne on 15 June 1527; after 1540 the Ming received tribute from both the Lê and the Mạc, which continued through the Qing; in 1597 the Ming recognized the Lê monarch; in 1667 the Kangxi Emperor gave Lê Duy Vũ the title An Nam Quốc Vương; the dynasty ended in 1789.

mac-dynasty.title: Mạc dynasty (Wikipedia)
mac-dynasty.supports: In 1540 Mạc Đăng Dung was downgraded from emperor to governor (đô thống sứ); after 1540 the Ming received tribute from both the Lê and the Mạc; Thăng Long lost in 1592, then Cao Bằng; after the Southern Ming both became Qing tributaries (infobox: Qing 1662-1677); in 1667 Kangxi demanded Cao Bằng be returned to the Mạc; the dynasty ended in 1677.

trinh-lords.title: Trịnh lords (Wikipedia)
trinh-lords.supports: The Trịnh treated the Qing as they had treated the Ming emperors, sending tribute and formal acknowledgements; only the Lê ruler, not the Trịnh lord, met the Qing's diplomats.

tay-son.title: Tây Sơn dynasty (Wikipedia)
tay-son.supports: In 1789 the Qianlong Emperor agreed to re-establish the tributary relationship and enfeoff Nguyễn Huệ as King of Annam; infobox: within the Qing tributary system, 1789-1802.

amasya.title: Peace of Amasya (Wikipedia)
amasya.supports: Agreed on 29 May 1555; eastern Georgia stayed in Iranian hands and western Georgia fell in Ottoman hands, under native vassal princes.

kartli.title: Kingdom of Kartli (Wikipedia)
kartli.supports: Infobox: vassal of Persia 1555-1578, 1612-1723 and 1736-1747, of the Ottoman Empire 1578-1612 and 1723-1736; Kartli under vassalage of successive dynasties of Persia; Rostom appointed king (wali) in 1632; de facto independence after Nader Shah's death (1747); united with Kakheti in 1762.

kakheti.title: Kingdom of Kakheti (Wikipedia)
kakheti.supports: Infobox: vassal of Persia 1555-1578, 1612-1723 and 1736-1747, of the Ottoman Empire 1578-1612 and 1723-1736 (a yearly tribute of 30 bales of silk from 1578); the Peace of Amasya (1555) left it in the Safavid sphere; successive Ottoman and Iranian occupations 1724-1744; Nader Shah's grant of 1744; united with Kartli in 1762.

safavid-georgia.title: Safavid Georgia (Wikipedia)
safavid-georgia.supports: Kartli and Kakheti Safavid vassals from the 1510s; the Ottoman invasion of 1578; the Treaty of Zuhab (1639) reconfirmed them as Iranian domains; the Treaty of Constantinople (1724) gave Georgia back to the Ottomans; Nader deposed the Safavids in 1736.

kartli-kakheti.title: Kingdom of Kartli-Kakheti (Wikipedia)
kartli-kakheti.supports: 1762-1801; Erekle II's de jure submission to Karim Khan Zand and investiture as vali (infobox: 1762-1763); the Treaty of Georgievsk (24 July 1783) made the kingdom a Russian protectorate, abjuring any dependence on Iran; annexed by Paul I's decree of 18 December 1800, confirmed on 12 September 1801.

galicia.title: Kingdom of Galicia-Volhynia (Wikipedia)
galicia.supports: Daniel submitted to Batu as a vassal in the winter of 1245/46 (allegiance pledged 1246) and his house paid the Horde tribute; still tributary in 1308-1323; the Polish conquest of 1349 ended its vassalage to the Golden Horde (the infobox's 1246-1253 disagrees with the body).
